quote: The reason for choosing one strike OTM (out of the money) calls or puts during morning sessions is to balance risk and reward. This approach isn’t as risky as going far OTM, and it offers more reward potential than an ITM (in the money) trade. Plus, if the price moves against your idea, it won’t go as far, so the contract’s value doesn’t decay as quickly. In terms of risk/reward, it’s often the best choice.

That’s actually a really good observation — and it’s exactly what happens when someone tries to mirror another trader’s entries in real time.

This is one of the main reasons we always remind everyone that this isn’t a signal group, it’s an education community designed to teach you how to fish on your own.

During the live sessions, Coaches explain their full reasoning — the levels they’re watching, the confluences they need, and the reaction they’re waiting for. If someone still finds it hard to identify those same moments on their own charts, it’s usually a sign they should avoid trading real money for now and instead paper trade while studying how those setups form and play out.

The goal is to reach the point where you can spot and execute those same setups by yourself, without needing to rely on someone else’s timing — that’s where true growth and confidence as a trader begin.

author: Neto Moreno (Performance Coach)
quote:
Hey <@1216920932937896040>,
Quick clarification on my risk approach (since I trade only SPY 0DTE, always the same setup, same asset, same expiration, and same 1OTM strike every time):
Because everything is so consistent (same playbook, same contract type, same Greeks behavior), I know exactly how price moves, how fast it runs, and how often it hits my typical stop zone. That deep familiarity lets me comfortably accept a wider stop-loss — usually 18–25% of the contract premium at entry — without it feeling scary or reckless.

**It’s not “risking more for no reason”** — it’s risking more because the setup is ultra-predictable for me after thousands of reps. 
Losses in that range are boring and expected; they don’t rattle me or blow up my day. 
When the trade works (which it does often enough), the Greeks kick in hard and the payoff more than covers it.

Bottom line:
Consistency in setup + asset + expiration + strike lets me widen the stop safely and still keep my fixed dollar risk per trade the same every day.
Your own number will come from your data — track your exact setup long enough, see what % premium loss feels “normal” vs. emotional, and build from there.
Hope that makes more sense! Keep grinding — you’re asking the right questions.

Personally, I think most traders dramatically overestimate how many opportunities they need.

I trade exclusively SPY. Many days I only take 1–2 trades. Some days I take none.

The issue is usually not a lack of opportunities.
The issue is a lack of patience and a lack of confidence in a repeatable process.

If you've spent a year watching QQQ, there is real value in that. Familiarity matters. You start recognizing behavior, rhythm, and structure much faster than someone constantly jumping between tickers.

Adding more tickers can help if you're looking for more occurrences of the same setup.

But adding more tickers will not solve execution problems.

A lot of traders think:
"I need more opportunities."

When the real problem is:
"I don't consistently execute the opportunities I already have."

If I were in your position, I wouldn't force myself to expand right now.

I would ask:
Can I become consistently profitable trading only QQQ?

If the answer is no, adding 5 more tickers probably won't fix it.

The good news is that SPY and QQQ provide opportunities almost every single week, especially if you're focused on the first 1–2 hours after the open.

No setup → no trade.

I'd rather see a trader become extremely good at one instrument than average at ten.

For me, the biggest mechanical shift wasn't one specific rule—it was changing my mindset from "How much can I make?" to "How much am I willing to lose if I'm wrong?"
**Every decision started with risk first.**

Looking at your journal, I'd focus on #1 before anything else. A poor entry usually forces a wider stop or gets you stopped out before the move develops.

Position sizing simply amplifies whatever execution you already have. If the execution isn't consistent yet, adding contracts will only magnify the mistakes.

That's why I always tell traders: earn the right to size up.

author: Neto Moreno (Performance Coach)
quote:
I think you already answered your own question.

If your system can't explain why you took 15 contracts instead of 30, then position sizing is discretionary.

Personally, I don't increase size just because I "feel" more confident about a trade.
Position size should come from predefined rules, not emotions.

My advice would be to define exactly what conditions justify each size. If you can't write those rules down before the trade, I'd keep the size consistent until you can.

Consistency in execution starts with consistency in risk.

author: Neto Moreno (Performance Coach)

That usually tells me it’s not a chart-reading problem—it’s a confidence in execution problem.

If 80% of those trades are reaching your target, start collecting data on your A+ setups. The more evidence you build that your edge works, the easier it becomes to trust yourself when it’s time to click the button.

Confidence doesn’t come before execution. It comes from repeatedly executing your plan.

I consider Premarket from **4:00 AM EST until the market opens at 9:30 AM EST.**

As for VWAP, I actually don’t use it—or any other indicators. My trading is based almost entirely on **market structure, key levels, liquidity, and price action.**

author: Neto Moreno (Performance Coach)
quote:
I actually try not to count confluences.

For my Playbook, I’m looking for a sequence that tells the same story:
• Failure to create new highs.
• Momentum shift.
• Market structure shift to the downside.
• Support turns into resistance.
• HTF levels supporting the thesis.

If those pieces are aligned, that’s usually an A+ opportunity for me.

That’s not meant to be a universal checklist. It’s simply what I’ve found works best through my own data and experience. My advice is to build your own Playbook and let your own data define what an A+ setup looks like for you.

author: Neto Moreno (Performance Coach)
quote:
It depends on what you’re trying to validate.

If you’re learning to read price action in real time, replaying candle by candle can be a great exercise because it forces you to make decisions without knowing what’s coming next.

If your goal is to collect data on a specific setup, though, you don’t necessarily need to replay every candle. You can review historical charts, identify occurrences of your setup, and document what happened. That tends to be much faster.

The key is to be intentional. Don’t just “backtest”, know exactly what question you’re trying to answer.

author: Neto Moreno (Performance Coach)
quote:
For me, it came down to reducing variables.

By focusing on one ticker, I learned its behavior, stopped jumping between charts, and spent my time getting better at execution instead of constantly searching for the next opportunity.

Since you only have the first 30 minutes to trade, specializing in one ticker like SPY could absolutely make sense. It lets you spend less time scanning and more time understanding how that instrument behaves.

You can always expand later, but there’s nothing wrong with mastering one thing before adding more.

author: Neto Moreno (Performance Coach)
quote:
Great question. Personally, I make all of my execution decisions based on the underlying (SPY), not the option chart.

Options have additional variables (delta, implied volatility, spread, time decay) that can cause the premium to behave differently than the underlying.

My entries, stops, targets, and trade management all come from the SPY chart. The option is simply the vehicle I’m using to express that idea.

That’s what has worked best for my trading. Others may incorporate the option premium into their management, but I prefer to keep my decision-making centered on the underlying.

author: Neto Moreno (Performance Coach)
quote:
That’s a tough stretch, but I’d start by asking a different question:

Has the market changed, or has your execution changed?

If your trade reviews are consistently coming back as A/B-quality trades, then it may simply be a losing streak. Those happen in trading.

But if you’re forcing trades, relaxing your criteria, or taking setups that don’t fully match your Playbook, then the issue is execution—not probability.

Either way, this is when risk management matters most. Your goal isn’t to make the losses back quickly. It’s to stay in the game long enough for your edge to play out over a large sample of trades.
